title: 3-Read Friday #102: Cognitive Realism, Engelmann, and an AI Summit
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #102 leads with Barbara Oakley's debut Substack post, in which she argues that constructivism's unfalsifiable structure has allowed ineffective discovery-based teaching to persist despite contrary evidence, and proposes 'cognitive realism' -- evidence-accountable instruction aligned with how the brain actually learns -- as the necessary corrective. Dylan Kane then argues that Zig Engelmann's most important legacy is not Direct Instruction itself, but his process of obsessive content analysis and relentless empirical testing, an approach teachers and curriculum designers should adopt to move beyond generic pedagogy toward content-specific, evidence-driven instruction. Dan Meyer closes by reporting from Stanford's AI+Education Summit that the field is sobering up to the reality that AI tools risk harming learning and self-belief, arguing -- as with MOOCs before it -- that technology cannot substitute for the human relationships at the heart of effective education. Barton's own framing treats Oakley's launch as a genuine event worth celebrating alongside the week's other picks.
points: Oakley's 'cognitive realism' argument: constructivism's unfalsifiable structure lets discovery-based teaching survive contrary evidence, so instruction should instead be held accountable to evidence about how the brain actually learns.

Kane relocates Engelmann's legacy away from Direct Instruction-as-brand and toward his underlying method -- obsessive content analysis plus relentless empirical testing -- as the transferable lesson for curriculum designers.

Meyer's Stanford Summit report signals a field-wide sobering on AI in education: tools risk harming learning and self-belief, and -- echoing the MOOC era -- cannot substitute for the human relationships that drive learning.
Barton treats a first-time Substack launch (Oakley's) as newsletter-worthy in its own right, a signal of how much weight he places on her arrival in the space.
